vignette:
The Weight of the Waiting Room

David is a 63-year-old internist who has spent the better part of four decades learning how to stay calm when other people cannot. He is the kind of doctor who remembers his patients' children's names, who sits on the edge of the exam table rather than behind the desk, who has always believed that medicine is, at its core, an act of presence. That belief was tested — and in some ways broken — on an afternoon three years ago when a pipe bomb detonated in the lobby of the downtown medical complex where he keeps his practice.

He was between appointments when it happened. The sound, he says, was not what he expected. It was less like an explosion and more like the building itself inhaling sharply. Then the ceiling tiles came down, and the lights went out, and there was screaming from somewhere he could not locate. He moved toward it — because that is what he does — and found two of his colleagues on the floor, a receptionist with a laceration across her forearm, and a man he did not recognize who was not moving. David worked on that man for eleven minutes before paramedics arrived. The man survived. David does not talk about those eleven minutes easily, and when he does, he speaks in the clipped, technical language of someone trying to keep a safe distance from the memory.

In the months that followed, David told his wife, Carol, that he was fine. He told his partners at the practice the same thing. He returned to work within two weeks, which felt, to him, like evidence of resilience. What he did not tell anyone was that he had begun arriving at the office before the cleaning staff, before any patients, before anyone could be in the lobby when he walked through it. He stopped using the main entrance altogether, entering instead through a side door near the parking garage. He told himself it was more convenient.

Sleep became unreliable. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart already racing, the details of the dream dissolving before he can hold them, leaving only the physical residue — the sweat, the tightness in his chest, the sense that something is still happening. Carol has learned not to reach for him in those moments. He needs a few minutes, he says. He goes to the kitchen and reads.

At work, he is competent and present, but his staff has noticed that he startles at sounds — a door slamming, a cart rolling across tile — in ways he did not before. He has become, without quite meaning to, a physician who keeps one eye on the exit. When the waiting room is crowded, something tightens in him that he cannot name clinically, though he suspects he could if he tried. He does not try.

He has grown quieter at home. Carol describes him as "somewhere else" even when he is sitting across from her at dinner. He knows she is right. He finds it difficult to care about things that used to matter — the garden he planted every spring, the Saturday morning runs he shared with his son-in-law, the medical journal articles he once read for pleasure. There is a flatness to his days that he attributes, when pressed, to aging, to burnout, to the cumulative weight of a long career.

What David has not yet fully allowed himself to consider is that the man he was before that afternoon — the one who walked through the front door without thinking, who slept through the night, who felt at home in the building where he had practiced for thirty years — may have needed help long before now. He sits in the same chair where he has listened to thousands of patients describe their pain, and he is only beginning to learn how to describe his own.
